study_identification.author_journal_year: Ma et al., Journal of Behavioral Addictions, 2024
study_identification.title: Comparative analysis of cortical anatomy in male participants with internet gaming disorder or tobacco use disorder: Insights from normative modeling

study_characteristics.study_objective: To apply normative modeling to analyze cortical thickness (CT) development patterns in male patients with Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD) and Tobacco Use Disorder (TUD), comparing individual-level deviations to provide insights into whether IGD qualifies as an addiction by examining similarities and differences with TUD.

dataset_name.reason: The healthy control data were explicitly downloaded from the Brain Genomics Superstruct Project (GSP), a large-scale, multi-site brain imaging study.
dataset_name.supporting_text: In addition, data of 665 male participants were downloaded from the Brain Genomics Superstruct Project (GSP), a large-scale, multi-site brain imaging study (Holmes et al., 2015). Each site participating in the GSP had obtained informed consent from the participants (view at https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/25833) prior to their enrolment.

imaging_modality.reason: The MRI acquisition section clearly specifies that high-resolution T1 structural images were acquired.
imaging_modality.supporting_text: High-resolution T1 structural images were acquired on a 3 Tesla Siemens Trio scanner using a fast spoiled gradient-recalled echo pulse sequence with magnetization preparation, which encompassed the entire brain (176 slices).

analysis_level.reason: The analysis is explicitly performed at the ROI level using the Desikan-Killiany atlas. The paper states ROI-level t-tests were performed, and limitations acknowledge the ROI-wise rather than vertex-wise approach.
analysis_level.supporting_text: CT data, based on the Desikan-Killiany atlas, were obtained for each participant through cortical surface reconstruction (Fig. 1B). The mean group differences were determined by performing ROI-level t-tests on the z-scores of the three cohorts. Limitations: 'the analysis was performed on an ROI-wise rather than vertex-wise basis.'

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: CAT-12; SPM-12; Desikan-Killiany atlas; Surface-based brain morphometry (SBM)
preprocessing_pipeline.reason: The preprocessing pipeline is clearly described, including CAT-12 toolbox for surface-based brain morphometry integrated in SPM-12, with cortical parcellation using the Desikan-Killiany atlas.
preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: Raw MRI images were processed and analyzed using surface-based brain morphometry (SBM) pipeline available in the CAT-12 toolbox (Gaser, Nenadic, Buchsbaum, Hazlett, & Buchsbaum, 2001). The images were then integrated in the statistical parametric mapping version 12 (SPM-12) (Fig. 1B) and subjected to pre-processing steps. The volumes were subsequently segmented using surface-based and thickness estimation techniques to analyze specific regions of interest. Cortical parcellation was conducted using the Desikan-Killiany atlas (Desikan et al., 2006).

quality_checking.reason: Quality control was performed using two metrics: weighted average IQR (Image Quality Rating) assessed by CAT-12 and Euler index with site-specific thresholds. Exclusion numbers are reported for each group.
quality_checking.supporting_text: The quality control process was performed by referring to the weighted average IQR assessed by the CAT-12 toolbox, which provides a comprehensive evaluation of the cortical surface reconstruction quality. All participants with IQR ratings below 'C-' were excluded (no participants were excluded in HC, while 8 were excluded in the IGD and 1 in the TUD). CAT-12 also calculates the Euler index, which tallies the instances when the toolbox has interpolated surface gaps during the process of reconstruction to ensure a continuous outcome surface... we subtracted the median Euler index of each site from every participant within it, then took the square root and multiplied by −1, and excluded participants with square roots greater than 10. Finally, we manually examined participants that exceeded the Euler index threshold to confirm their exclusion from further processing (no participants were excluded in HC, while 2 were excluded in the IGD and 6 in the TUD).

quality_checking_detail.answer: Two-stage QC process: (1) IQR threshold (exclude below 'C-'): HC 0 excluded, IGD 8 excluded, TUD 1 excluded; (2) Euler index site-wise median-centered with sqrt threshold >10 followed by manual verification: HC 0 excluded, IGD 2 excluded, TUD 6 excluded. Total exclusions: IGD 10, TUD 7, HC 0.
quality_checking_detail.reason: Detailed QC metrics, thresholds, and exclusion counts are explicitly reported for both stages of quality control.
quality_checking_detail.supporting_text: All participants with IQR ratings below 'C-' were excluded (no participants were excluded in HC, while 8 were excluded in the IGD and 1 in the TUD)... we subtracted the median Euler index of each site from every participant within it, then took the square root and multiplied by −1, and excluded participants with square roots greater than 10. Finally, we manually examined participants that exceeded the Euler index threshold to confirm their exclusion from further processing (no participants were excluded in HC, while 2 were excluded in the IGD and 6 in the TUD).

site_effect_handling.reason: Site effects were not handled through traditional batch-removal (ComBat) or explicit model-based approaches (site as covariate/random effect). Instead, site-related differences were addressed indirectly through site-wise Euler index normalization and quality control. The Euler index (used as a model covariate) is noted to be closely related to scanning site.
site_effect_handling.supporting_text: As the Euler index is closely related to the scanning site, we followed the approach proposed by Rutherford et al. to apply a consistent exclusion threshold across different sites. In this approach, we subtracted the median Euler index of each site from every participant within it, then took the square root and multiplied by −1, and excluded participants with square roots greater than 10.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Site effects mitigated indirectly through: (1) site-wise median-centering of Euler index with sqrt(|Euler_median_centered|)>10 exclusion threshold to ensure consistent quality across sites; (2) Euler index included as a covariate in the normative model, which is 'closely related to the scanning site'. No explicit ComBat harmonization, hierarchical Bayesian regression with site random effects, or site fixed-effect modeling was applied.
site_effect_handling_detail.reason: The paper describes site-related quality control through Euler index normalization following Rutherford et al.'s approach and notes that Euler index (a model covariate) is related to site, but does not implement traditional site effect handling methods.
site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: As the Euler index is closely related to the scanning site, we followed the approach proposed by Rutherford et al. to apply a consistent exclusion threshold across different sites. In this approach, we subtracted the median Euler index of each site from every participant within it, then took the square root and multiplied by −1, and excluded participants with square roots greater than 10... The Predictive Clinical Neuroscience toolkit (PCNtoolkit) was used to estimate a normative model of CT and predict the entire brain based on participants' age and euler index as covariates.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: Nuisance structure was partially addressed. Image quality (Euler index) was included as a covariate and used for site-wise QC, addressing some aspects of measurement quality and site-related variance. However, there is no explicit modeling of heteroscedasticity, site/scanner as random or fixed effects, or other batch variables. The GPR provides prediction uncertainty estimates, which helps with variance modeling, but specific handling of complex nuisance structures (e.g., site-specific variance parameters, non-linear age effects by site) is not described.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: ... based on participants' age and euler index as covariates. As the Euler index is closely related to the scanning site, we followed the approach proposed by Rutherford et al. to apply a consistent exclusion threshold across different sites... To directly compare the deviations of the cohorts, parameters were estimated using training data with empirical Bayesian estimation.

clinical_dataset.answer: Locally recruited male participants with IGD and TUD (recruited at Center for Cognition and Brain Disorders, Hangzhou Normal University)

diseases_studied.answer: Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD); Tobacco Use Disorder (TUD)

clinical_groups_n.answer: IGD: 68 (after QC from initial 78); TUD: 71 (after QC from initial 80)

clinical_groups_age.answer: IGD: mean 21.46; sd 2.22; min 19; max 29. TUD: mean 22.13; sd 1.80; min 19; max 26

deviation_metric.answer: ROI-wise z-scores from normative model. Extreme deviations defined at |z| ≥ 2.6 (p < 0.005) for primary mapping of extreme values; also examined at |z| ≥ 1.65 (p < 0.05) for spatial distribution of deviations. Subject-level abnormality index: percentage of extreme positive and negative deviations across all ROIs.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Partial Spearman correlation analysis (FDR-corrected, p < 0.05) between regional z-score deviations and addiction severity scores (DSM-5 criteria count and IAT for IGD; FTND and QSU for TUD), controlling for gender, head motion, and Euler index. ROI-level t-tests with Bonferroni-Holm correction (p < 0.05) for group comparisons of z-scores.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Both IGD and TUD exhibit widespread cortical thinning with significant overlap in bilateral temporal pole and medial orbitofrontal cortex; TUD shows greater individualization and heterogeneity; opposite CT deviation trends observed in bilateral pericalcarine cortex and pars triangularis.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Both addiction groups showed widespread negative deviations (cortical thinning) compared to HC. IGD showed significant positive deviations in bilateral frontal pole (t=10.31/10.35, p<0.001) and right superior parietal cortex (t=3.34, p<0.001). TUD showed positive deviations in bilateral frontal pole (t=4.11/6.11, p<0.001) and bilateral lateral occipital cortex (t=3.65/6.40, p≤0.001). Both groups exhibited significant negative deviations and high proportions of extreme deviations in bilateral temporal pole (IGD: Z=-1.82/-1.59; TUD: Z=-2.00/-2.22) and medial orbitofrontal cortex (TUD: Z=-1.76). TUD demonstrated higher proportions of extreme ROIs (positive: 20.59% [14/68]; negative: 73.53% [50/68]) compared to IGD (positive: 8.82% [6/68]; negative: 42.65% [29/68]). Opposite deviation patterns: in pericalcarine cortex, IGD showed negative deviation (t=-7.82/-6.48, p<0.001) while TUD showed positive deviation (t=3.35, p=0.003 left; t=0.965, ns right); in pars triangularis, IGD showed positive deviation (right: t=2.50, p=0.041) while TUD showed negative deviation (t=-4.97/-4.40, p<0.001). Correlations: IGD DSM scores positively correlated with deviations in left entorhinal cortex (r=0.27, pFDR=0.029), right lateral orbitofrontal cortex (r=0.25, pFDR=0.041), right parahippocampal gyrus (r=0.25, pFDR=0.004), and right frontal pole (r=0.26, pFDR=0.036). TUD FTND scores negatively correlated with deviations in left lateral orbitofrontal cortex (r=-0.24, pFDR=0.047), right medial orbitofrontal cortex (r=-0.38, pFDR=0.001), right rostral anterior cingulate cortex (r=-0.28, pFDR=0.016), right rostral middle frontal gyrus (r=-0.25, pFDR=0.039), left superior parietal cortex (r=-0.29, pFDR=0.015), and left superior temporal cortex (r=-0.27, pFDR=0.023).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: ROI-wise rather than vertex-wise analysis may lose more local information; other addictions excluded only through verbal inquiry without scale/biochemical data for intergroup comparisons; GSP dataset does not provide IGD/TUD diagnoses, so some HC participants may have these conditions despite large sample size; cross-sectional design limits ability to validate developmental trajectories—longitudinal validation warranted.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Normative modeling preserves case-control group-level paradigm while providing individual-level insights. Normative probability maps (NPMs) quantify multivariate deviations across all brain regions. Thresholds (|z|≥2.6 for extreme mapping, |z|≥1.65 for spatial distribution) were chosen to reduce sensitivity to overall deviation changes compared to FDR correction. Subject-level abnormality index (percentage of extreme deviations) provides summary score. Empirical Bayesian parameter estimation used to directly compare cohort deviations. Findings suggest IGD shares neurobiological alterations with substance-related addictions (TUD), supporting its classification as addiction, while also revealing disorder-specific patterns and greater heterogeneity in TUD.

general_notes.general_notes: MRI scanner: 3 Tesla Siemens Trio. Acquisition parameters: TR=2000ms, TE=3ms, slice thickness=1.0mm (no gap), flip angle=7°, TI=1100ms, FOV=256×256mm, in-plane resolution=256×256. Enrollment: IGD n=78 recruited, TUD n=80 recruited; after matching and QC: IGD n=68, TUD n=71, HC n=665. IGD diagnosis: ≥5 DSM-5 criteria + IAT>50. TUD diagnosis: ≥10 cigarettes/day for ≥1 year + exhaled CO≥5ppm + FTND>4 + QSU-B>15. Age/education matching performed using MatchIt package in R with non-parametric nearest neighbor matching. Both patient groups recruited from local sites in China; HC from multi-site GSP dataset. Ethical approval from Hangzhou Normal University. Analysis software: CAT-12, SPM-12, PCNtoolkit, Python 3.8. Statistical corrections: Bonferroni-Holm for ROI-level t-tests; FDR for correlation analyses. Desikan-Killiany atlas provides 68 cortical ROIs (34 per hemisphere). Study highlights individual heterogeneity masked by group averages, demonstrating value of normative modeling for personalized addiction research.
